ENT CLINICAL NOTE 

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint/trigger: Two-day history of wheeze and shortness of breath after heavy dust exposure while cleaning carpet at home.  
- Symptom timeline/progression: Onset ≈1 h after exposure; gradual worsening over 48 h; notably worse at night; today unable to finish sentences at times.  
- ENT-related symptoms: 
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation – not reported  
  • Voice change/hoarseness – not reported  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling – denied  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms – none currently (does report seasonal hay fever in summer)  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing – denies stridor; reports expiratory wheeze  
  • Dyspnea – present (mild–moderate, worsens with speech)  
  • Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling – none  
  • Ear pain/hearing changes – not reported  
  • Neck pain/swelling – not reported  
- Relevant past episodes/treatments: Childhood asthma (occasional exertional flare as adult); keeps a short-acting inhaler (not used in this episode). Has previously taken oral steroids for asthma (dates/doses not documented). No prior ED visits for anaphylaxis.  
- Allergies & medications:  
  • Drug/food allergies – none known  
  • Current meds – none regular  
  • Rescue meds – Salbutamol inhaler (dose/strength/frequency not documented); has NOT used it for current episode. No antihistamines at home.  
- Social context: At home alone during video call; GP surgery ~10 min drive away.

Objective:
- Visible swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): None observed/reported.  
- Airway/breathing: Patient able to speak in full sentences initially but reports needing pauses; no stridor heard over call.  
- Mental status: Alert, oriented; denies dizziness or syncope.  
- Vitals & physical exam: Not recorded (video feed lost; no on-call equipment).  
- Companion present: None.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Likely allergen-triggered asthma exacerbation vs. lower-airway allergic reaction secondary to dust exposure. Airway currently stable but risk of deterioration without treatment.  
  Evidence: childhood asthma history, clear temporal link to dust, progressive nocturnal wheeze, short phrases on speech, absence of fever or infection signs.  
- Relevant DDx (from reasoning system, consistent with history):  
  1. Asthma exacerbation (High likelihood) – prior asthma, classic triggers/symptoms, nocturnal pattern.  
  2. Acute allergic bronchospasm to dust mite antigen (Medium) – hay-fever history and irritant exposure; lacks upper-airway/skin findings.  
  3. Viral bronchitis (Medium-Low) – possible but no cough, fever, or systemic signs.  
  No conflicting information noted.

Plan:
- Immediate: Advised patient to attend local GP/urgent care today for objective assessment (pulse oximetry, peak-flow, possible spirometry).  
- Medications prior to review: Obtain and take an OTC non-sedating antihistamine en-route if available. Bring and consider using salbutamol inhaler per usual asthma action plan (not yet utilized).  
- Possible in-clinic management discussed: Short course oral corticosteroid if objective findings confirm asthma flare (decision deferred to in-person clinician).  
- Education & red-flags: Seek emergency help (999) if any of the following develop: increased breathlessness, inability to speak full words, chest/t throat tightness, audible wheeze/stridor at rest, facial or tongue swelling, dizziness/syncope. Remain accompanied until reviewed.  
- Follow-up: Letter sent via app to GP summarizing consultation and recommending same-day review. Suggested formal asthma review and consideration of dust-mite avoidance measures and regular preventer therapy if diagnosis confirmed.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Objective vitals (RR, HR, SpO₂), peak-flow reading, inhaler name/strength/dose, exact past steroid details, full allergy list, smoking status.  
● Transcript vs DDx conflicts: None identified.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief video dropout limited visual examination.
